summary: At 77 people per square mile spread across 2,152 square miles, Madera County is physically enormous — stretching from the flat, irrigated farmland of the San Joaquin Valley floor all the way up into the Sierra Nevada high country, where a significant eastern slice of the county actually falls inside Yosemite National Park. That geographic range means a resident near the city of Madera looks out at open-sky agricultural horizons, while someone in the foothill communities around Oakhurst lives among ponderosa pines at 2,000-plus feet, serving as a primary gateway to Yosemite Valley. The economy runs on agriculture, timber, and the service jobs that Yosemite tourism generates; the county is not a major job center for professional or knowledge-economy roles, and many workers commute south to Fresno along Highway 99. Housing looks approachable on paper — a median home value of $367,700 against a median household income of $75,496 yields a price-to-income ratio under 5:1 — but a poverty rate near 20% signals that affordability is uneven and wage floors in the dominant industries stay low. With 9.4 hours of daily sunshine and summer highs that bake the valley side well past the listed 68°F annual average, the climate splits sharply between a hot, dry lowland and a cooler mountain zone. Madera is essentially two counties stitched together by elevation — one agricultural and commuter-oriented, the other wild and tourist-facing — and which version you'd live in matters more than the county name on the address.
